blocks.text: II. The second passage is 1 Reg. IV, 23. [var. V, 3.], where among Solomon's provisions [col. 112] are reckoned ברבורים אבוסים, that is, תרנגולין פטומין, fattened cocks, as it is found in Selomo, whom Pagninus follows. Likewise for Pomarius and Aquinas ברבור barbur is תרנגול סריס, a castrated cock, that is, a capon. Nor do the Greek translators depart far from this; here they have ἐκτὸς ὀρνίθων ἐκλεκτῶν νομάδων [ektos ornithōn eklektōn nomadōn], besides choice pasture-fed hens. I prefer this to rendering it, as others do, besides birds, etc. For although ὄρνιθες [ornithes] are often birds in general, yet for the Greek translators, as for the Evangelists, a bird is ὄρνεον [orneon], and a hen is ὄρνις [ornis]. Moreover, ὄρνις νομὰς [ornis nomas] is nothing other than a fattened or pasture-fed hen. In Nicander's Alexipharmaca, line [II, 678] 295, there is βοσκὰς ὀρταλὶς [boskas ortalis], where the Scholiast has νομὰς ὄρνις [nomas ornis], the very words of the Greek translators. And in Artemidorus's Ὀψαρτυτικά [Opsartytika], as cited by Athenaeus, book 14, chapter 23: Νομάδα παχεῖαν ἕψε, καὶ νεοσσοὺς τῶν ἤδη κοκκυζόντων [Nomada pacheian hepse, kai neossous tōn ēdē kokkyzontōn]; Boil a fat pasture-fed hen, and, of the chicks, those that already crow. So it must be rendered, not, as the translator most ineptly has it, a fat dove, etc., and of the chicks those that still peep. For the subject is a mattya to be made from a hen. Accordingly it is immediately added: Εἶτ᾽ ἐξελὼν τὰ λάχανα εἰς τρυβλίον, καὶ τῆς ὄρνιθος τῶν κρεῶν ἐπιθεὶς [Eit᾽ exelōn ta lachana eis trublion, kai tēs ornithos tōn kreōn epitheis]; Then taking out the vegetables, put them into a dish, and placing the hen's meat on them. And ἤδη [ēdē] does not mean still, but already. Nor is κοκκύζειν [kokkyzein] proper to doves, but to cocks, as is clear from Aristophanes, Aristotle, Theocritus, Aelian and Lucian. For it is an onomatopoeic word, like the vernacular coq for the cock, which we name thus from its crowing. Finally, νομὰς [nomas] is a hen, yet not a Numidian one, as the most learned commentator would have it, but a pasture-fed one. Others call them σιτιστὰς [sitistas] or σιτευτὰς [siteutas]. Athenaeus, book 14, chapter 21: Σιτιστῶν δὲ ὀρνίθων μὲν μνημονεύει Μάτρων ἐν ταῖς Παρῳδίαις οὕτως [Sitistōn de ornithōn men mnēmoneuei Matrōn en tais Parōdiais houtōs],
Ὣς ἔφαθ᾽, οἱ δ᾽ ἐγέλασσαν, ἐπήνεγκάν τ᾽ ἐπὶ τούτῳ Σιτευτὰς ὄρνιθας ἐπ᾽ ἀργυρέοισι πίναξι· [Hōs ephath᾽, hoi d᾽ egelassan, epēnenkan t᾽ epi toutō Siteutas ornithas ep᾽ argyreoisi pinaxi]

Matron mentions fattened hens thus in his Parodies: When he had said this, they laughed, and then brought in fattened hens on silver platters. I say fattened hens with Metellus, the Pontifex Maximus, whose words are in the description of the pontifical dinner in Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 3, chapter 13: Before the dinner, sea urchins, raw oysters, as many as they wished, giant clams, spondyli, a thrush, asparagus, and beneath it a fattened hen. Nor did Pliny mean anything else by the term altilia when he said of the seed of the tamarisk, book 24, chapter 9: Applied with the fat of fattened fowls to boils. Cato had said pascales; whence Festus: Both sheep and hens are called pascales, because they graze about everywhere. Pascales, that is, νομάδες [nomades], as altiles are σιτισταὶ [sitistai] or σιτευταί [siteutai]. Thus in the view of the Greeks ברבורים אבוסים are pasture-fed or fattened hens. And that some of the older Hebrews held the same view is found in Selomo. This, however, can by no means be held as certain and established, since there is no word whose meaning is more disputed, as we shall show below in a chapter devoted to that word.
